title: Security, Architecture & Polish: The Final Cleanup
excerpt: Token security, repository refactoring, environment variable hygiene, and the many small fixes that separate a prototype from a product.

content.markdown:
After the major features shipped, we turned our attention to the invisible work — security hardening, architectural cleanup, and the long tail of small fixes that make an app feel finished.

## Token Security

GroupHub uses a dual-token strategy: a short-lived access token (30 minutes) for API requests and a long-lived refresh token (30 days) stored in an httpOnly, signed cookie. The refresh token is exchanged silently on 401 responses, so users stay logged in across sessions without ever exposing a long-lived token to JavaScript.

### Separate Secrets for Separate Concerns

Originally, the same `JWT_ACCESS_SECRET` was reused for email verification tokens and password reset tokens. This meant compromising one secret would break all three systems. We introduced `JWT_EMAIL_SECRET` and `JWT_RESET_SECRET` as optional overrides, falling back to the access secret when not set — backward compatible but encouraging separation.

### Token Expiry Tuning

We went through three iterations:
- **Original**: 15m access / 7d refresh — users complained about frequent logouts
- **First fix**: 365d both — secure? No. A leaked cookie is valid for a year
- **Final**: 30m access / 30d refresh — the sweet spot between security and comfort

The frontend's silent refresh mechanism handles the 30-minute expiry transparently. Users never notice the access token rotating.

## Repository Layer Refactoring

The matchmaking service was the last holdout using direct Mongoose model calls instead of the repository layer. `User.findById()`, `Project.find()`, and `ProjectMembership.find().distinct()` were all called inline in the service logic.

We extracted these into repository methods:
- `userRepository.find(filter)` — generic find with lean
- `projectRepository.find(filter)` — same pattern
- `membershipRepository.findProjectIdsByUser()` / `findUserIdsByProject()` — distinct queries
- `roleRepository.countOpenByProjectId()` — single-project counterpart to the existing multi-project method

This means every database operation now goes through the repository layer, making it easy to add caching, audit logging, or query optimization in one place.

## Environment Variable Hygiene

The env schema had 8 dead configuration variables: `AI_PROVIDER`, `REDIS_URL`, `REDIS_TOKEN`, and `SENTRY_DSN` were defined but never referenced anywhere in the code. `LOG_LEVEL` was referenced in the logger but missing from the schema entirely. We removed the dead vars, added `LOG_LEVEL`, and updated `.env.example` to match exactly what's consumed.

## The Small Fixes

A production app lives in its details. We fixed:

- Array index keys in the PillInput component
- A JSX syntax error where `const statIcons` was embedded inside markup instead of JavaScript scope
- Missing `topThree` state declaration causing a runtime ReferenceError on the leaderboard
- Read-only email input that was still focusable (now `tabIndex={-1}`)
- ARIA attributes on modals for accessibility
- Native `confirm()` and `alert()` calls replaced with inline feedback
- About page demo content replaced with real team information

## Documentation Reorganization

All markdown documentation was consolidated into a `documents/` directory and added to `.gitignore`. The repository now tracks only source code — architectural plans, session notes, and design documents live alongside the project but don't pollute the git history.

## Wrap Up

This sprint was about making GroupHub production-ready. Not through any single feature, but through dozens of small, deliberate improvements to security, architecture, and user experience.

lessons: Don't reuse the same JWT secret for different token types
30m/30d is the right token expiry balance for most web apps
Every database call should go through a repository layer
Remove env vars that are defined but never consumed
